s0302: At that time wishing to expand agriculture, Xi submitted a memorial saying: He was transferred to Assistant Editorial Director, compiled the Jinshu Basic Annals and the Ten Treatises, was promoted in turn to Erudite, and continued in his editorial duties as before.

This line reads like two unrelated strands fused in transmission: an opening about expanding farming policy (possibly corrupt—the phrase is sometimes emended in relation to Xi’s courtesy name, Guangwei 廣微) followed without transition by standard résumé sentences. Sense of the second part: Shu Xi was moved to Assistant Editorial Director, helped compile the Jinshu annals and ten treatises, advanced to Erudite, and kept his editorial post.
s0303: Formerly, a man of Ji Commandery named Bu Zhun broke open the tomb of King Xiang of Wei—some say it was the mound of King An of Li—and obtained bamboo documents filling dozens of carts.
Long ago, Bu Zhun of Ji Commandery looted the burial mound of King Xiang of Wei—or, some claimed, of King An of Li—and hauled out bamboo slips by the cartload.
s0304: Its Bamboo Annals in thirteen sections records events from Xia down to King You of Zhou’s destruction by the Quanrong; it connects the narrative to subsequent events, through the tripartite partition of Jin, and continues to relate Wei affairs down to the twentieth year of King An of Li.

The Bamboo Annals, thirteen scrolls, runs from the Xia age to King You’s fall to the Quanrong; it picks up the thread through the three houses’ partition of Jin and carries Wei’s story to the twentieth year of King An’s reign.
s0305: Generally speaking, this Wei state history largely corresponds with the Spring and Autumn Annals in many particulars.
Broadly, Wei’s chronicle and the Spring and Autumn Annals align on many points.
s0306: Where its classics and commentaries diverge greatly, it claims the Xia reign-years exceeded those of Yin;
Where text and gloss part company sharply, it asserts Xia’s calendar ran longer than Shang’s;
s0307: Yi seized Qi’s throne; Qi killed him;
Yi wrested the throne from Qi; Qi slew him;
s0308: Tai Jia put Yi Yin to death;
s0309: King Wen Ding executed Ji Li;
s0310: From Zhou receiving the Mandate down to King Mu was one hundred years—it does not mean King Mu lived one hundred years;
From Zhou’s receipt of Heaven’s charge to King Mu spans a century—not that Mu himself lived a hundred years;
s0311: After King You perished, a certain Elder He of Gong acted as regent in the Son of Heaven’s affairs—it was not the joint regime of two ministers.
When King You fell, Elder He of Gong held the royal interim—not the dual stewardship miscalled ‘Joint Harmony.’
s0312: Its Changes Classic in two sections matches the Zhouyi upper and lower classics.
Its two-scroll Changes parallels the Zhouyi’s upper and lower wings.
s0313: Its Yi Yaoyin Yang Hexagrams in two sections broadly resemble the Zhouyi, but the Yaoci texts differ.
The pair titled Yi Yaoyin Yang Hexagrams roughly tracks the Zhouyi while its line texts diverge.
s0314: Its Hexagram-subordinate Changes Classic in one piece resembles the Shuogua but is not the same.
The piece called Hexagram-subordinate Changes looks like the Shuogua yet departs from it.
s0315: Its Gong Sun Duan in two sections: Gong Sun Duan disputing the Changes with Shao Zhi.
Two scrolls of Gong Sun Duan record his debate on the Changes with Shao Zhi.
s0316: Its Discourses of the States in three sections speaks of Chu and Jin affairs.
Three scrolls of Discourses of the States treat Chu and Jin.
s0317: Its Names in three sections resembles the Record of Rites, and also resembles the Erya and Analects.
Three scrolls titled Names echo the Record of Rites and recall the Erya and Analects.
s0318: Its Shi Chun in one piece records the divinations from the Zuo Tradition; ‘Shi Chun’ seems to be the compiler’s name.
Shi Chun, one scroll, collects Zuo-style oracle readings; the title likely memorializes its author.
s0319: Its Suoyu in eleven sections is a composite of states’ dream omens, prodigies, and physiognomy writings.
Eleven scrolls of Suoyu gather omens, dreams, and fate lore from many lands.
s0320: Its Liangqiu Zang in one piece first narrates Wei’s reign-counts, then speaks of hill-store gold and jade.
Liangqiu Zang opens with Wei’s generations, then turns to treasure buried in the mound.
s0321: Its Jiaoshu in two sections discusses archery by trailing cord.
Two scrolls of Jiaoshu expound the trailing-line hunt.
s0322: Its Sheng Feng in one piece lists what emperors enfeoffed.
s0323: Its Great Calendar in two sections belongs with Master Zou’s talks on heaven.
Two scrolls of Great Calendar belong to the astronomizing school of Zou Yan.
s0324: Its Mu Tianzi Zhuan in five sections describes King Mu of Zhou roaming the four seas, visiting the Terrace of the Emperor and the Queen Mother of the West.
Five scrolls of Mu Tianzi Zhuan follow King Mu across the seas to the Emperor’s terrace and Xiwangmu’s realm.
s0325: Its Tu Shi in one piece belongs to the genre of painted encomia.
Tu Shi is of the picture-caption kind.
s0326: Further sundry writings nineteen pieces: Zhou Field-allotment Law, Zhou Documents, On Chu Affairs, The Death of King Mu of Zhou’s Beauty Sheng Ji.
Nineteen miscellanies follow—field law, Zhou documents, Chu affairs, and the death of King Mu’s favorite Sheng Ji.
s0327: Altogether seventy-five pieces; seven bamboo bundles were broken and illegible, their titles unknown.
Seventy-five titles in all; seven slip-bundles snapped beyond reading, names lost.
s0328: From the tomb also came one bronze sword, two feet five inches long.
They also pulled a bronze blade two feet five inches from the mound.
s0329: The lacquer writing was all in tadpole script.
Every character was lacquered tadpole script.
s0330: At first the grave-openers burned slips for light to seize valuables; when officials recovered them, many were charred, snapped, or shredded—the text was ruined and could no longer be ordered.
Looters torched bamboo for light; when the state salvaged the haul, char and breaks left the text unsalvageable for collation.
s0331: Emperor Wu handed the cache to the Palace Library to stitch sequence and repair breaks, trace intended meaning, and transcribe it into modern script.
The emperor entrusted the bundle to the secretariat for restoration, sense-finding, and conversion into current graphs.
s0332: While Xi held his editorial post he could inspect the bamboo texts; wherever doubt arose he analyzed and glossed, each point grounded in evidence.
As editor, Xi studied the slips firsthand, resolving doubts with argued readings.
s0333: He was promoted to Gentleman of the Masters of Writing.
He rose to Gentleman of the Masters of Writing.
s0334: Emperor Wu once asked Zhi Yu the meaning of the third-day winding-water rite; Yu replied: ‘In Zhang of Han’s reign, Xu Zhao of Pingyuan bore three daughters on the third of the third month; all three died that day; the villagers thought it uncanny and led families to the stream to wash and exorcise; hence floating cups on the water—the custom began thus.

The emperor quizzed Zhi Yu on ‘winding water’ on day three. Yu’s tale: during Han Zhangdi, Xu Zhao of Pingyuan’s triple birth on the double-third ended in triple death; villagers drew kin to the bank for ablution, then cups rode the current—that, he said, was the origin.
s0335: ’ The emperor said: ‘If it truly began so, it was no happy thing.
The throne answered: If your story is true, the custom began in grief, not joy.
s0336: ’ Xi stepped forward: ‘Yu is young and cannot know; allow your servant to speak.
Xi interjected: The lad lacks breadth—I will explain.
s0337: Formerly the Duke of Zhou completed Luoyi and floated wine along the flowing water; thus lost Odes lines say “feather goblets drift with the waves.
When the Duke of Zhou finished Luoyi he let cups ride the current—hence the stray verse, ‘feathered cups on the wave.’
s0338: Again King Zhao of Qin on the third day set wine at the river’s bend and saw a golden man present a sword from the water’s heart, saying: ‘May my lord rule Western Xia.
King Zhao of Qin feasted at the river bend on day three and saw a golden figure offer a sword from midstream: ‘You shall master Western Xia.’
s0339: ’ Then he lorded it over the feudatories; on that account he established winding water.
Thus he rose above the lords—and founded the winding-water gathering.
s0340: The two Han dynasties carried it on in succession; each held splendid assemblies.
Both Han courts continued it as grand festivals.
s0341: ’ The emperor was greatly pleased and granted Xi fifty jin of gold.
The sovereign delighted and weighed out fifty jin of gold for Xi.
s0342: At that time someone found beneath Song Mountain a single bamboo slip with two lines of tadpole script; it was passed hand to hand and none could read it.
Then a lone slip surfaced under Songshan—two lines nobody could decipher.
s0343: Minister of Works Zhang Hua showed it to Xi; Xi said: ‘This is the cedar-text from Emperor Ming’s Xianjie mausoleum.
Zhang Hua brought it to Xi, who declared it the cedar-plaque wording from Mingdi’s Xianjie tomb.
s0344: ’ Inspection proved him right; people of the time admired his vast learning.
Verification bore him out; contemporaries bowed to his erudition.
s0345: Prince Zhao of Zhao serving as Chancellor of State invited Xi to be his secretary.
When Prince Lun of Zhao held the chancellorship he asked Xi to join his secretariat.
s0346: Xi pleaded illness, resigned, and returned home to teach disciples.
Xi pleaded sickness, withdrew, and taught students.
s0347: He died at forty; Yuanshi ward silenced its trades for him; pupils and old friends raised a stele beside his grave.
He fell at forty; Yuan district stilled its markets; disciples and friends carved stone at his mound.
s0348: Xi’s talents ranged wide; his Three Wei Worthies Biography, Seven Dynasties Comprehensive Record, Jinshu Annals and Treatises—all were lost in turmoil.
His oeuvre—Three Wei Worthies, Seven Dynasties overview, Jin annals and treatises—vanished in the wars.
s0349: His Five Classics Comprehensive Discussion, Primers Record, Supplementary Lost Odes, and collected writings in several tens of pieces circulated in the world, it is said.
What survived reputedly included his Five Classics synthesis, Primers, patched ‘lost’ odes, and dozens of collected pieces.
s0351: Wang Jie, courtesy Zuyou, was a man of Yishi in Hedong, tenth-generation descendant of Han’s Metropolitan Governor Wang Zun.
Wang Jie, styled Zuyou, from Yishi in Hedong—the tenth generation down from Wang Zun, Han’s capital intendant.
s0352: His father Wei practiced Confucian and historical scholarship for generations.
His father Wei sustained generations of classical and historical learning.
s0353: Wei Commandant-in-Chief Cao Xi wrote On Utmost Impartiality; Wei praised it and composed On Utmost Pivot; its phrasing was very fine.
Palace Army commander Cao Xi’s Utmost Impartiality impressed Wei, who answered with Utmost Pivot—language of rare polish.
s0354: His office reached Marquis of Xiayang’s chancellor.
He rose to magistrate for the Marquis of Xiayang.
s0355: Jie lost his father while young; his grief exceeded ritual measure; neighbors sighed: ‘The Wangs have a true son!
Orphaned young, Jie mourned past the rites; neighbors murmured, The Wang line has an heir.
s0356: ’ Liu Yuan of Bohai, serving as Hedong governor, loved the unusual and made displaying talent his task.
Liu Yuan of Bohai, as Hedong governor, courted wonder and hunted talent.
s0357: Feng Shou of the same commandery passed the classics examination and became a gentleman; past seventy he recommended Jie to Yuan, saying: ‘If fine steeds wear no gathered reins, they are not in Zaofu’s stable;
Co-provincial Feng Shou, a classics-tested gentleman past seventy, urged Yuan: ‘Unbitted bays never reach Zaofu’s yard;
s0358: if the bright moon sheds no flowing light, it is not in Marquis Sui’s palm.
Moonlight unfelt never rests in Sui Hou’s hand.’
s0359: I humbly consider that Your Honor embraces virtue at the yellow center and shines with doubled li’s clarity; you seek worth and ability without overlooking the smallest talent—therefore this rustic elder wishes to offer what he knows.
He trusts Your Honor’s centered virtue and luminous clarity; you miss no gifted soul—so this old man offers a name.
s0360: Privately I have observed the recluse Wang Jie: precocious and outstanding, orphaned at thirteen, observing mourning with full propriety; learning—once seen, understood; principles—touching one class, he lengthened all—this is the subtle savor of the jade tripods’ handle, the fine plan that orders the age.
The witness: young Jie, brilliant, bereaved at thirteen yet ritually perfect—reads once and grasps, infers wide—the savor of the sacred tripods, policy for an era.
s0361: I do not worry that black grain will not open; I privately rejoice that spring blossoms arrive in season.
I do not fret that night grain fails to sprout—I rejoice spring blooms on time.
s0362: ’ Yuan immediately sent ritual summons; Jie would not accept.
Yuan dispatched formal invitation; Jie declined.
s0363: Yuan then called him in and said: ‘Do you wish to emulate the lofty reclusion of Fei?
Yuan summoned him: Do you chase Fei’s lofty withdrawal?
s0364: ’ He replied: ‘Jie has thin fortune, was orphaned young without brothers, and his mother is aged and gravely ill—therefore he has no heart for office.
Jie answered: Little blessing left me fatherless and brotherless with a dying mother—office holds no lure.
s0365: ’ When his mother died, he wasted to bones by grief; he dwelt by the tomb for years, exhaustively reading many books and producing many divergent interpretations.
When she passed he withered beside her mound for years, reading widely and arguing fresh glosses.
s0366: His nature was plain and direct; he cultivated no fashionable conduct; great local clans mostly could not warm to him—only Pei Yi truly understood him.
Plain-spoken, indifferent to fashion, grand families spurned him—only Pei Yi saw his worth.
s0367: Pingyang governor Liu Dan, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Pei Xia, and Supervisor of the Masters of Writing Deng You were all friendly with Jie.
Governor Liu Dan of Pingyang, attendant Pei Xia, and minister Deng You counted him friend.
s0368: Later he became county clerk for documentation; welcoming Governor Wen Yu, Yu marveled at him and transferred him to merit clerk.
He served as county registrar, impressed incoming Governor Wen Yu, and became merit clerk.
s0369: The province summoned him as Pingyang adjutant.
The province appointed him Pingyang staff officer.
s0370: At that time Yang Liang of Taishan was Pingyang governor; he recommended Jie to Metropolitan Governor Wang Kan, who appointed him assistant for capital affairs.
Taishan’s Yang Liang, then Pingyang governor, pushed Jie to Wang Kan, who gave him a capital-affairs post.
s0371: At the beginning of Yongning he was nominated cultivated talent.
In Yongning’s opening year he earned the ‘cultivated talent’ nomination.
s0372: His friend Pan Tao of Xingyang sent Jie a letter: ‘Zhi Yu and Bian Xuanren both say you should harmonize the tripods’ savor—can you ignore the cultivated-talent summons?
Friend Pan Tao wrote: Zhi Yu and Bian Xuanren say you belong at the cauldron—will you spurn nomination?
s0373: ’ Jie answered: ‘In this age the Way lies ruined in mutual ruin; stripping and chaos will follow; wise men seal lips and sheathe brushes; calamity deepens daily like fire spreading across the plain—can it be saved?
Jie replied: The age rots toward collapse; the wise shut mouth and pen while disaster spreads like flame—who can stem it?
s0374: It is not glory that drives this journey; I wish only to lay out what I see, hoping for awakening.
Not for glory—I mean to speak plain truth and wake someone.
s0375: ’ That year the three princes raised the righteous host; Emperor Hui resumed the throne; because the state had great celebration, all nominated ‘cultivated’ and ‘filial’ candidates nationwide went untested—Jie considered it a regret.
That year the three princes revolted; Hui returned; national jubilee waived exams for every nominee—Jie mourned the lost trial.
s0376: He was appointed gentleman of the palace and supplemented Attendant General Who Subdues Captives’ marshal.
He took gentleman rank and filled Subduing Captives general’s staff marshal.
s0377: In the Battle of Dangyin, Palace Attendant Ji Shao was killed by mutinous troops; Jie argued: ‘One who plots another’s army—when the army fails, dies for it;
At Dangyin, mutineers slew Ji Shao; Jie argued: Plot another’s host—fail and die with it;
s0378: one who plots another’s state—when the state is imperiled, perishes for it: the ancient way.
plot another’s realm—peril it and perish: antiquity’s rule.
s0379: In the Dangyin affair the hundred officials fled north; only Ji Shao held his post against lawlessness—he may be called a minister, and may be called heartbreaking.
While courtiers ran, Shao stood his ground against outrage—a minister and a wound.
s0380: Now the eastern march plans a great campaign; it should proclaim lofty integrity to command the realm.
The east readies war—signal supreme fidelity to rally the world.
s0381: Following the Spring and Autumn’s praise of threefold accumulation of merit, add to Shao the reward due one who gave his life—then far and near will turn like wind and none dare show disrespect.
Apply Spring and Autumn praise for triple merit; crown Shao’s martyr’s wage—then all quarters heed.
s0383: Prince of Hejian Sima Yong wished to move the imperial carriage to Chang’an; discord with the eastern alliance—because Jie was Chengdu Prince’s aide he held it difficult and memorialized a transfer to county chancellor for the Prince of Linfen.
Hejian wanted the court in Chang’an, at odds with the east; Jie, Chengdu prince’s assistant, balked and was rotated to Linfen prince’s county chief.
s0384: When Prince of the Eastern Seas Sima Yue led the lords against Yong, Masters of Writing chief Wang Kan headed the mobile directorate and memorialized Jie as Gentleman of the Palace Masters of Writing—before he arrived he died, aged thirty-nine.
When Donghai Yue marched on Yong, minister Wang Kan’s field headquarters nominated Jie as palace secretary—he died en route at thirty-nine.
s0385: Though Jie’s learning was vast, he especially excelled at the Rites and Traditions.
Erudite broadly, he shone on Rites and Zuo.
s0386: He often said the Zuo language is rich in gloss and sense—its own book, not chiefly composed to open the classics.
He held Zuo its own literary cosmos—not mainly a key to the classics.
s0387: The Gongyang anchors gloss to classic; what the classic omits, gloss does not invent—literarily spare, for penetrating the classics it excels.
Gongyang ties commentary to text; silence in canon stays silence in gloss—lean prose, excellent for threading the classics.
s0388: Rencheng He Xiu’s commentary is minute yet demotes Zhou and enthrones Lu—broadly skewed—and though intent on Gongyang he often becomes Gongyang’s ailment.
He Xiu of Rencheng glosses minutely yet demotes Zhou for Lu—warped—and his Gongyang zeal breeds Gongyang’s own sickness.
s0389: Jie therefore reannotated Gongyang’s Spring and Autumn, often with fresh senses.
So Jie rewrote Gongyang with many new readings.
s0390: At that time Palace Library Assistant Wei Heng was collating the Ji tomb texts but had not finished when disaster struck.
Secretariat aide Wei Heng edited the Ji cache unfinished when calamity hit.
s0391: Assistant Editorial Director Shu Xi carried it to completion, many points verified with divergent readings.
Editor Shu Xi finished the job, evidence often clashing.
s0392: At that time Chenliu Wang Tingjian, governor of Donglai, challenged it; he too had proofs.
Donglai governor Wang Tingjian of Chenliu disputed him—with documentation.
s0393: Xi answered the challenge, but Tingjian had already died.
s0394: Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Pan Tao told Jie: ‘Your talent and reason suffice to settle the two men’s quarrel—essay it.
Pan Tao urged: Your learning can end their feud—write it out.
s0395: ’ Jie then detailed their merits and faults.
s0396: Zhi Yu and Xie Heng were both broadly learned; both deemed it fair.
Zhi Yu and Xie Heng, encyclopedic, called it just.
s0397: He also compiled Later Biographies of Exemplary Women, seventy-two figures, mixed essays, rhapsodies, dirges, stele hymns, and polemics exceeding one hundred thousand graphs—all lost in chaos.
He authored seventy-two Later Exemplary Women plus essays, fu, eulogy, stele, debate—over hundred thousand graphs—gone in war.
s0398: His eldest son Qianqi drifted south of the Yangzi; following his father’s intent he reannotated Gongyang and reassembled Later Exemplary Women.
Eldest son Qianqi fled south and, honoring his intent, re-glossed Gongyang and recollected the women’s sequel.
s0400: The historians say: Huangfu Mi walked a plain path in secluded integrity; dwelling retired he nursed illness, lavishing care on brush-cut ink, devoted to ancient learning—carriage-and-cap honor could not tempt him, poverty and low estate did not shame him—steadfastly unmoved: surely among Jin’s lofty recluses!
The editors: Huangfu Mi kept plain virtue in quiet withdrawal—ink for illness, joy in tombs—unswayed by rank or poverty: a Jin-era recluse among recluses.
s0401: When he framed ‘Earnest Endings,’ preaching thin burial and revealing thrift—warning extravagance like the Ji clan yet rejecting Prince Yang’s stance—he may be called one who grasped the hinge of life and death.
His ‘Earnest Endings’ essay favors humble graves—scorning Ji excess yet avoiding Yang’s nihilism—seeing clear through mortality’s door.
